The fog didn’t roll in; it collapsed. One moment the Atlantic was a churning sheet of black glass, the next, it was a wall of wet wool pressing against the lantern room’s thick panes.

Elias wiped his hands on a rag that had seen better decades. He was seventy-two, his joints clicking like the rusted gears of the clockwork mechanism he kept wound every four hours. The light swept out, a rhythmic *thrum-thrum* that vibrated in his teeth.

Then, the radio crackled. Not the static hiss of interference, but a voice. Clear. Dry. Terrifyingly familiar.

"Elias. Don’t wind the clock."

Elias froze, his hand hovering over the brass crank. He knew that voice. It was his own, stripped of the gravel and age, sharp with panic.

"Who is this?" Elias shouted into the receiver, though he knew the answer. The frequency was dead air. No one used this channel.

"Listen to me," the voice said, breathless. "The storm isn’t a storm. It’s a breach. If you wind the clock, the light stays on. If the light stays on, *they* see the door.
